notes:
I have gathered substantial material from Enduring Word (Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic), Gill (older Baptist), Ellicott (Anglican), Matthew Henry (older Presbyterian), Constable, and others. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

# Ezekiel 37 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Part 1: The Vision of the Valley of Dry Bones (vv. 1–14)

### v. 1 — "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and He brought me out by His Spirit and set me down in the middle of the valley, and it was full of bones."

- **The "hand of the LORD"** indicates prophetic ecstasy and divine inspiration. Ezekiel was not physically transported but was taken in vision. The phrase signals a powerful impulse of God's Spirit upon the prophet. (Gill: "a powerful impulse of his upon the prophet; the Targum interprets it a spirit of prophecy"). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- **"In the Spirit of the LORD"** — this was a visionary experience, not a physical relocation. Guzik notes, "We regard what follows as something Ezekiel saw as a vision, not with his physical sense of sight." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **The valley (Heb. *biq'ah*)** is the same word as the "plain" in Ezekiel 3:22, probably the same location where Ezekiel had earlier visions. Ellicott notes this and adds that the definite article suggests the same plain. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **Full of bones** — Not heaped but thickly strewn on the surface. The bones lay exposed like corpses denied proper burial, which was a shocking disgrace in ancient Israel. As a priest, Ezekiel would have been especially sensitive to the dishonour of unburied remains. (Guzik, citing Block and Taylor) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **Symbolism:** Bones are the framework of the body. Precept Austin notes that in context, the bones represent the framework of the nation of Israel coming to life, not individual bodies. The nation, Jerusalem, and the Temple all lay in ruins at the time. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary

### v. 2 — "He led me all around among them, and I saw a great many bones on the floor of the valley, and indeed, they were very dry."

- **"He caused me to pass by them round about"** — multiple times around, so Ezekiel could take exact notice of their number and condition. Gill: "several times round, that he might take exact notice of them, of their number, situation, and condition." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- **"Very dry"** — this signifies that a long time had passed since life departed. The dryness removed any natural possibility of life returning. Ellicott: "as showing that it was a long time since life had left them, and that the possibility of their living again was far removed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **On the surface** — The bones were not buried in graves. This is a necessary feature of the vision so they could be seen. (Precept Austin, Ellicott) — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary
- **Spiritually**, Gill notes these dry bones are an emblem of men in an unregenerate state: dead in trespasses, with no spiritual sense, no strength to redeem themselves, no inward desires after God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 3 — "Then He asked me, 'Son of man, can these bones come to life?' 'O Lord GOD,' I replied, 'only You know.'"

- **The question** is designed to emphasise the human impossibility of the situation, so that what follows is clearly a work of divine omnipotence. Ellicott: "The question is put to the prophet in order to emphasise the human impossibility of that which is immediately brought about by the Divine omnipotence." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **Ezekiel's answer** is carefully balanced. Guzik notes three things: (1) Ezekiel had no hope in the bones, but he did have hope in God. (2) He did not presume to know what God wanted to do. (3) He was confident that God did know. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Gill adds that the prophet knew that neither he nor any creature could quicken them, so he wisely refers the matter to an omniscient and omnipotent God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- Matthew Henry summarises: "No created power could restore human bones to life. God alone could cause them to live." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/37.htm

### v. 4 — "And He said to me, 'Prophesy concerning these bones and tell them, "Dry bones, hear the word of the LORD!"'"

- **"Prophesy"** here means "speak on God's behalf" — it does not necessarily carry the idea of prediction but of proclamation. (Ellicott) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **Preaching to dead bones** seemed foolish by human logic, yet God commanded it. Guzik invokes Spurgeon: "If we want revivals, we must revive our reverence for the Word of God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Gill notes that even unconverted sinners may be preached to; they are capable of hearing with bodily ears, and "faith comes by hearing." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- The address "O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD" is striking — the word of God has power to address that which is utterly dead.

### v. 5 — "This is what the Lord GOD says to these bones: I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life."

- **"Breath"** — the Hebrew word is *ruah*, which can mean breath, wind, or spirit depending on context. (Ellicott, Constable) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- God promises what only He can do. Gill: "none could do this but the living God, who breathed the breath of life into Adam at first, and he became a living soul; to which there seems to be an allusion here." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- This was a work of *revival* — restoring life to something that once had life, not creating life from nothing. (Guzik) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/

### v. 6 — "I will attach tendons to you and make flesh grow upon you and cover you with skin. I will put breath within you so that you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the LORD."

- **The stages are described in the order of creation in reverse:** first the framework (bones), then connective tissue (sinews), then flesh, then skin. Block, cited by Guzik: "The sequence involving bones, sinews, flesh, and skin reflects an understanding of anatomy available to anyone who had witnessed the slaughter of an animal; it also reverses the decomposition process." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **The purpose:** "Then you will know that I am the LORD." This is a recurring theme in Ezekiel — God acts so that His people and the nations will recognise Him. Precept Austin notes "I will" appears 177 times in 137 verses in Ezekiel. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary
- Gill notes that when men are called by grace, they come to know the Lord in a way they did not before — by experiencing His powerful and efficacious grace on their hearts. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 7 — "So I prophesied as I had been commanded. And as I prophesied, there was suddenly a noise, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone."

- **Ezekiel's immediate obedience:** "So I prophesied as I was commanded." He did not argue; he obeyed, however foolish the act seemed. Guzik: "If Ezekiel had any doubts, he put them away and did what God commanded." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **"A noise, a rattling"** — Gill notes this was *the first prophesying* (to the bones), distinct from the second (to the breath). Different effects followed each. In the literal/historical sense, Gill associates the "voice" with the proclamation of Cyrus giving the Jews leave to return. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- **"Bone to his bone"** — the bones assembled properly into correct skeletons, not random assemblages. Guzik: "When God restores, He puts things together in the right way." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Spurgeon, cited by Guzik, notes that we should value every movement of the Spirit's power, even before there is full life: "the shaking and the noises, and the coming of the sinews and the flesh, even before there was any sign of life." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/

### v. 8 — "As I looked on, tendons appeared on them, flesh grew, and skin covered them; but there was no breath in them."

- **Two-stage restoration:** Ellicott notes the two stages have "evident reference to the record of the creation of man in Genesis 2:7." First, the body is formed perfectly; second, breath gives life. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"But there was no breath in them"** — they had form and structure but no life. Gill compares this to Adam's body before God breathed life into it, and to those who "have the form of godliness, and appear outwardly righteous before men, submitting to ordinances, and performing the duties of religion; and yet no principle of spiritual life in them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- Guzik makes a key point: this demonstrates that the work of revival happens in stages. The stirring and assembling of the bones, then the flesh, then the skin — and yet still awaiting the breath of God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Feinberg, cited by Guzik: "There is no teaching in the Scriptures that the resurrection of anyone from physical death will take place in stages, such as is stated here." This argues that the vision is about national restoration, not individual physical resurrection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/

### v. 9 — "Then He said to me, 'Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and tell the breath that this is what the Lord GOD says: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!'"

- **The second prophecy** — now directed not to bones but to the *ruah* (breath/wind/Spirit). Taylor, cited by Guzik: "The second action was tantamount to praying, as Ezekiel besought the Spirit of God to effect the miracle of re-creation, to breathe into man's nostrils the breath of life (cf. Genesis 2:7). This time the effect was devastating. What preaching by itself failed to achieve, prayer made a reality." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **"Come from the four winds"** — from every direction, indicating a comprehensive gathering. Constable connects this with Isaiah 43:5-6 and Jeremiah 31:8 about gathering from all directions. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-37.html
- Spurgeon, cited by Guzik: "First, the prophet prophesies to the bones – here is preaching; and next, he prophesies to the four winds – here is praying." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **"These slain"** — the word is used designedly. Ellicott: "The bones which Ezekiel had seen were those not merely of dead, but of slain men; and in this was their likeness to Israel: as desolated, and their nationality for the time destroyed by their enemies." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- Gill notes that the ancient Jews in the Zohar applied the "breath" or "spirit" here to the Spirit of the Messiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 10 — "So I prophesied as He had commanded me, and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet—a vast army."

- **Immediate obedience again:** Ezekiel prophesied to the wind "as He commanded me." The result was that breath/the Spirit entered them and they lived. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- **"An exceeding great army"** (KJV) — the Hebrew is very emphatic: "a power, or great host, very, very great" (Poole, cited by Guzik). They did not rise to be spectators but to be soldiers under orders. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Gill sees this fulfilled at multiple levels: the Jews returning from Babylon (many and in a posture of defence), the converted Jews in the latter day (Hosea 1:10), and the saints at the first resurrection (Revelation 7:9). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- Guzik: "With all word and no spirit, we can be an army of the dead – assembled, solid, but without the true breath of life." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/

### v. 11 — "Then He said to me, 'Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off."'"

- **The divine interpretation:** This verse is the key. "These bones are the whole house of Israel." Ellicott says this "leaves no doubt of its meaning. Whatever other sense might possibly be attached to its language, there can be no uncertainty as to that which the Spirit intended." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"Whole house of Israel"** — not just Judah (the southern kingdom) but also the northern tribes scattered by Assyria 150 years earlier. Guzik: "It might have surprised him when God revealed they represented the whole house of Israel, not only those from the kingdom of Judah." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **"Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished"** — this was the actual sentiment of the exiles. They felt utterly hopeless. Gill: "all the expressions show the desperate and despairing condition they were in." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- John MacArthur, cited by Precept Austin, says vv. 11-13 are "the key to the interpretation of the vision. It is the resurrection and salvation of Israel." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary

### v. 12 — "Therefore prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel.'"

- **"O My people"** — even in their desperate state, God still claims them as His. Gill: "they were his people still, and he had a covenant interest in them… all proceeded from his covenant, and the grace of it, and their relation to him." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- **Shift in imagery:** the bones were exposed on the valley floor in the vision (a necessity so they could be seen); now the people are spoken of as being in graves, "since this was the normal and proper place for the dead" (Ellicott). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"I will open your graves"** — Gill says the "graves" represent the cities and prisons in Chaldea where the Jews were confined as captives, out of which they could no more deliver themselves than a dead man can rise from his grave. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary interprets this as being "brought alive politically, from their national graves, as 'restoration' from the dead" (citing Romans 11:15). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-37.html
- **"I will bring you back to the land of Israel"** — the restoration is both spiritual and geographical. Matthew Henry says the vision predicts "both their restoration after the captivity, and also their recovery from their present and long-continued dispersion." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/37.htm

### v. 13 — "Then you, My people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them."

- **Knowing God through His acts:** The opening of graves is something only omnipotent God can do. When they experience it, they will "know, own, and acknowledge him." (Gill) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html
- The repetition of "O My people" (v. 12) and "My people" (v. 13) reinforces the covenant relationship as the basis for this restoration.

### v. 14 — "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD."

- **"I will put My Spirit in you"** — this connects directly to the great promise of Ezekiel 36:27. It is a reference to the Holy Spirit and regeneration. Precept Austin: "In the context of the previous chapter, this is clearly a reference to the Holy Spirit and the regeneration or new birth that only He can create (John 3:3, 5, 6, 7)." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary
- Ellicott notes the close association between moral resurrection and restoration to the land: "The former was at once the necessary condition of the latter, and would also be its consequence in a still higher development." He compares the similar association of spiritual with literal resurrection in John 5:21-29. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **Has this been fulfilled?** Guzik argues that "any fair examination of Israel's history must confess that it has not yet happened. This means that it is yet to be fulfilled, and will be fulfilled as part of God's plan for Israel in the very last days." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Matthew Henry sees multiple fulfilments: the return from Babylon, the ongoing conversion of sinners, and "a clear intimation of the resurrection of the dead." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/37.htm

## Part 2: The Two Sticks — Reunion of Israel and Judah (vv. 15–28)

### v. 15 — "Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,"

- This introduces a second, closely connected prophecy. Ellicott says it "probably was given very soon after the former." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- Precept Austin: "Ezekiel is not speculating or postulating but is proclaiming truth, performing the function of God's 'mouth piece.'" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary

### v. 16 — "And you, son of man, take a single stick and write on it: 'Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him.' Then take another stick and write on it: 'Belonging to Joseph—the stick of Ephraim—and to all the house of Israel associated with him.'"

- **"Stick"** — the Hebrew word is *'ets* (wood, piece of wood), not the word for "rod" used in Numbers 17. Ellicott: "the word here is an entirely different one, and means simply a piece of wood." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"For Judah and for the children of Israel his companions"** — this represents the southern kingdom: Judah, Benjamin, and those from other tribes who had aligned with them (cf. 2 Chronicles 11:16). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim"** — Joseph (father of Ephraim and Manasseh) represents the northern ten tribes. Ephraim is specified as the leading tribe. Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom, was an Ephraimite. (Clarke, cited by Guzik; Ellicott) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- Gill notes that writing on sticks may allude to Numbers 17:2, where rods were inscribed with names. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 17 — "Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand."

- Ezekiel was to hold the two sticks together so they appeared as one. Taylor, cited by Guzik: "His clenched fist will thus grasp the place where the two sticks meet, and it will appear as if he is holding one long stick in the middle." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Gill notes that some rabbis thought they miraculously became one, but it is enough that they appeared to be one. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 18 — "When your people ask you, 'Won't you explain to us what you mean by these?'"

- The symbolic action was designed to provoke curiosity. The people would ask its meaning — whether in sincerity or derision. Gill: "whether they would ask this seriously or in banter, out of curiosity or in contempt… it matters not, he was to give them an answer." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 19 — "you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel associated with him, and I will put them together with the stick of Judah. I will make them into a single stick, and they will become one in My hand.'"

- **"In the hand of Ephraim"** — contrasts human political power (Ephraim's leadership of the northern kingdom) with "My hand" (God's sovereign reunification). (Ellicott) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- The division that began under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12–14) will be healed. Guzik cites Trapp: "Taking away the deadly feud that hath so long time been between them, breaking down the partition wall." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/

### v. 20 — "When the sticks on which you write are in your hand and in full view of the people,"

- The united sticks were to remain visibly in Ezekiel's hand while he delivered the explanation. Ellicott: "The symbolical action was not only to be performed before the people, but the united wood was to remain in the prophet's hand, while he unfolded to them the Divine promise." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 21 — "you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: 'I will take the Israelites out of the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from all around and bring them into their own land.'"

- **A gathering far broader than the Babylonian captivity.** Guzik: "The restoration after the Babylonian exile was only a shadow of this promise. This was a promise to bring the Jewish people from among the nations, from a scattering much broader than the Babylonian captivity." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- Ellicott takes a different view: this restoration was fulfilled only to a "remnant," as Paul shows in Romans 9. A larger fulfilment "was perpetually prevented by the sins of the people; God did for them all that their obdurate disobedience would allow Him to do." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html

### v. 22 — "I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over all of them. Then they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms."

- **"One nation"** — the divided kingdom (since 931 BC) will be reunited. Precept Austin: "The kingdom of Israel which God divided in 931BC, He will one day (at the Second Coming) reunite into a single kingdom." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary
- **"One king"** — not merely a political leader but the promised Davidic ruler.

### v. 23 — "They will no longer defile themselves with their idols or detestable images, or with any of their transgressions. I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God."

- **Spiritual cleansing accompanies the physical restoration.** This is not merely a political regathering but a moral and spiritual renewal. The people will be purified from idolatry.
- **"I will save them from all their apostasies"** — Many Hebrew manuscripts (and LXX) read "all their apostasies" rather than "all their dwelling places." The BSB follows this reading in its footnote.
- **Covenant formula:** "They will be My people, and I will be their God" — the central promise of the covenants, echoing Leviticus 26:12, Jeremiah 31:33, and ultimately Revelation 21:3.

### v. 24 — "My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them. They will follow My ordinances and keep and observe My statutes."

- **"My servant David"** — here the major interpretive divide becomes most visible:
  - **Literal/futurist view (Guzik, Precept Austin):** David himself, resurrected, will rule as king over restored Israel. Guzik: "The promise of David ruling as king over restored Israel is presented straightforwardly as a literal future promise, not as coded language for the Messiah—if God said David, He meant David." Precept Austin: "I interpret this as a reference to a literal David, resurrected from the dead." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary
  - **Christological/typological view (Gill, Ellicott, Matthew Henry):** David is a type of Christ. Gill: "one King, Christ, the antitype of David." Ellicott: "David personally is described as their one king and shepherd" but notes the NT interprets such promises "of the everlasting reign of the King of kings, the Good Shepherd, over His people." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"One shepherd"** — echoes Ezekiel 34:23. The king and shepherd are one and the same.

### v. 25 — "They will live in the land that I gave to My servant Jacob, where your fathers lived. They will live there forever with their children and grandchildren, and My servant David will be their prince forever."

- **"Forever"** — this word is repeated with strong emphasis. Ellicott notes the repetition: the occupancy of the land is forever, David's kingship is forever, the sanctuary is "for evermore" (v. 26, 28), and the covenant is "an everlasting covenant" (v. 26). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"The land that I gave to My servant Jacob"** — the specific land promised to the patriarchs. A literal reading sees this as the geographical land of Israel. A figurative reading (Ellicott) sees the land promises as fulfilled in the "land of higher promise" in the new covenant.

### v. 26 — "And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant. I will establish them and multiply them, and I will set My sanctuary among them forever."

- **"Covenant of peace"** and **"everlasting covenant"** — Guzik notes this describes the new covenant, echoing Ezekiel 34:25, Isaiah 54:10, Ezekiel 16:60, and Hebrews 13:20. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/
- **"Multiply them"** — Ellicott interprets this as the increase of spiritual Israel: "Abraham was the father of all those who walk in his faith, whether they be of the circumcision or the uncircumcision (Romans 4:12)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- **"My sanctuary among them forever"** — the presence of God dwelling in the midst of His people.

### v. 27 — "My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people."

- **"My dwelling place"** (or "My tabernacle") — this verse is explicitly cited in 2 Corinthians 6:16: "For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, 'I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.'"
- Ellicott says this promise "in its reality began to be fulfilled at the incarnation of the Son of God, of whom it is said by St. John (John 1:14) that 'He dwelt (literally, tabernacled) among us,' and is continued by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 6:19)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html
- Matthew Henry: "Let us pray that all nations may be obedient and happy subjects of the Son of David, that the Lord may be our God, and we may be his people for evermore." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/37.htm

### v. 28 — "Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel, when My sanctuary is among them forever."

- **Witness to the nations:** God's purpose in restoring Israel is not only for Israel's sake but so that "the nations will know" — a missional purpose. The presence of God's sanctuary among His people demonstrates to the world that the LORD sanctifies Israel.
- This verse closes the chapter by returning to one of Ezekiel's great themes: the knowledge of the LORD spreading to the nations through His acts of restoration.

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Dispensational / Futurist (literal fulfilment for ethnic Israel)
- **Source:** David Guzik (Enduring Word — charismatic/Pentecostal background), Precept Austin, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary
- **View:** Ezekiel 37 predicts a future, literal restoration of ethnic Israel to the land, the reunification of the northern and southern kingdoms, and the reign of a resurrected David as king/prince. The return from Babylon was only a partial shadow. The full fulfilment awaits the end times. "If God said David, He meant David." (Guzik)
- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_37_commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-37.html

### Covenant / Amillennial / Figurative (fulfilled in Christ and the Church)
- **Source:** Charles Ellicott (Anglican)
- **View:** The Jewish Church and nationality have been "merged forever in the Church of Christ." The promises of land, Davidic kingship, and sanctuary are fulfilled typologically in Christ and spiritually in the Church. Ezekiel 37 is not about a future restoration of ethnic Israel but about the spiritual resurrection of God's people. NT usage (e.g., Acts 15:16 applying Amos 9:11-12 to Gentile-Jewish unity in the Church; 2 Corinthians 6:16 applying Ezekiel 37:27 to believers as God's temple) confirms this. The mention of Gog and Magog in Ezekiel 38–39 is likewise taken up figuratively in Revelation 20.
- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-37.html (especially the Excursus at the end)

### Classic Reformed / Puritan (both-and)
- **Source:** Matthew Henry, John Gill
- **View:** The vision refers first to Israel's return from Babylon, but also "was a clear intimation of the resurrection of the dead" and "represents the power and grace of God, in the conversion of the most hopeless sinners." Henry sees a threefold application: (1) return from captivity, (2) recovery from dispersion, (3) resurrection of the dead and conversion of sinners. Gill sees Christ as the antitype of David and also affirms a future conversion of the Jews.
- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/37.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### The Two-Stage Process (Word + Spirit)
- **Source:** Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist), cited extensively by Guzik; F.B. Meyer
- **View:** The two prophesyings teach that both the preaching of the Word and the prayerful invocation of the Holy Spirit are necessary for revival. Spurgeon: "What preaching by itself failed to achieve, prayer made a reality." This practical pastoral emphasis transcends the dispensational/covenant debate and is widely shared across traditions.
- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer

### Wesleyan/Methodist
- **Source:** Wesley's Notes (cited at Bible Hub)
- **Note:** Wesley's Notes describe the vision as "a representation of a threefold resurrection: Of the souls, from the life of righteousness: The church from an… to liberty and… of the body at the… day, especially the bodies of believers to life eternal." The full text could not be retrieved, but the excerpt suggests a multi-layered application.
- **URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/37.htm

## Other Views

### Mormon (Latter-day Saint) Interpretation
- **Mormonism teaches** that the two sticks represent the Bible (stick of Judah) and the Book of Mormon (stick of Joseph/Ephraim) being joined into one scriptural record. This view is explicitly rejected by the commentaries surveyed. Guzik cites Smith: "Certainly no basis exists in this text for the strange Mormon teaching that the sticks refer to two scrolls." Constable likewise refutes it, saying "the rest of the passage refutes this interpretation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-37/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-37.html

### Jewish Rabbinic Interpretations
- **Gill records several rabbinic views:** Some rabbis held there was a literal resurrection at the time of Ezekiel (R. Eliezer said the dead stood up, sang a song, and died; R. Eliezer ben R. Jose said they went to Israel, married, and had children). Gill dismisses these as "fabulous and romantic." Other rabbis understood the vision parabolically as the restoration from captivity. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-37.html

### Modern Scholarship
- **Could not retrieve** from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within search limits. ## Summary of Key Application Themes (Across Traditions)

1. **God's Word must be proclaimed even to what seems utterly dead** — Ezekiel's obedience in speaking to dry bones exemplifies faith in the supernatural power of God's Word.

2. **The Holy Spirit is indispensable** — preaching alone can assemble and structure, but only the Spirit gives life.

3. **Prayer completes what preaching begins** — the second prophecy (to the breath) represents intercessory prayer for the Spirit's empowering work.

4. **God restores in stages** — revival is often a process, not an instantaneous event.

5. **God's purpose is unity** — the divided sticks becoming one points to the healing of divisions among God's people.

6. **God's ultimate goal is His own glory and presence** — the refrain "then you/the nations will know that I am the LORD" and the promise of "My sanctuary among them forever" reveal that God acts for His name's sake and to dwell with His people.
